front: Who is better because I lead them?
back: My contribution includes what other people become. This week, choose one person on each team and ask what capability they want to build. Agree on one stretch responsibility, the support they need, and a follow-up. Measure the value from their side, too.
source: Adapted from John C. Maxwell — Law of Addition; personal application.

back: Before the week fills up, protect time for Megan, each daughter, and prayer or Bible study. At work, identify the decision or development conversation that needs my involvement. Delegate, defer, or drop something less important to make room. My priorities need time, not just agreement.
source: Adapted from John C. Maxwell — Law of Priorities; personal application.

back: Name the behavior → clear instruction → one warning → a related consequence → reconnect. Reconnect is not optional. It's the step that keeps the relationship intact after the correction.
Non-compliance, whining, disrespect. When I feel the heat rise, that's the cue to slow down, not speed up. Regulate myself first, then address the behavior.

front: Why my kids can trigger me like no one else
back: Two reasons: closeness (they live inside my boundaries) and projection (their behavior replays my own childhood). What I was shamed for as a kid — backtalk, whining, mess — is what will heat me up as a dad. If my reaction is bigger than the behavior, it's my history talking.
source: Jon Fogel — How to Not Lose Your Sh*t

back: Kids' brains can't multitask. Most "not listening" is "never actually heard you." Get full attention first — hand on shoulder, pause the tablet — then speak. And give the tablet back for a minute after, so my voice doesn't equal the fun ending.
source: Jon Fogel — How to Get Your Kid to Listen

back: Use the fewest words that carry the point. Every extra sentence dilutes the instruction and invites tune-out. One clear ask beats a lecture every time.

You can't out-chase what's more fun than you — the dog only came back when chasing stopped. Don't yell across the house; make coming to me safe, calm, and worth it. They ignore what's less interesting than what they're doing, so change the draw, not the volume.
Say the behavior I want, not the one I don't. "Feet on the floor," not "stop kicking." A brain hears the action either way — point it at the right one.
Don't praise generic good behavior — praise the moment she catches herself mid-frustration and changes course. That's the skill being built. Spotlight self-correction, and you get more of it.

front: Whining works — that's why they do it
back: Parents' brains are wired to find the whine sound impossible to ignore; it survives because it's effective. Distinguish attention-whining (teach the ask: normal voice gets the response) from complaining at a struggle (meet with empathy plus confidence, not rescue).

front: Sibling rivalry is a scarcity contest
back: Rivalry is natural and spikes where resources feel scarce — attention, who's first, who gets the ketchup. Same kids play great at the park. Reduce the contest (predictable turns, individual attention) instead of refereeing every skirmish.

1) Name and affirm: "Your anger is safe with me." 2) Stay near, even if told to go away. 3) Strong, safe limits: "You can be angry AND I won't let you hit." 4) Reflect and teach later, when calm. 5) Track her triggers so I'm regulated before it starts.
source: Julie Fragnito — Embracing Your Child's Anger

front: Anger prevention is 20 minutes a day
back: Twenty undistracted minutes in each daughter's world daily, predictable routines, all feelings allowed at home, lots of physical connection and laughter. Anger prevention is mostly presence, done in advance.

front: Boredom is a feature, not a problem
back: Don't fix it — tolerate it. Set clear expectations the day before, then let them whine through the discomfort. Boredom is where creativity, self-trust, and problem-solving grow. Solving it for them teaches them to depend on me for entertainment.

front: Emilia: the prompt is the threat
back: Her rejection is anxiety-driven, not sensory. "It's disgusting" is a preemptive shutdown — her nervous system reads the ask, not the food. Zero food pressure at the table: safe food always on her plate, new foods exist nearby without comment, meals stay easy.

When she tries something, react like it's any normal thing: "Oh yeah? What did you think?" Over-praising spotlights the act and raises the anxiety next time. New foods: one at a time, snack context first, 10–20 quiet appearances before judging.

front: Our marriage is their first relationship lesson
back: Kids absorb how we disagree. Disagree respectfully in the open — no slammed doors, no silent treatment — and let them see the apology and resolution too. Never let a child pick a side. And own my own mood: nobody else is responsible for it.

Life skills come from real missions — manage $10 at the grocery store, order at the counter, make eye contact and say thank you. Then reflect together: what did you learn about yourself? Experience plus reflection is the curriculum.
Acts of service and quality time. Small consistent gestures beat rare grand ones. Ask each day: what did I do that she'd actually feel?
The little things I let slide are the things she notices. Consistency is the gift. Earn it daily — don't coast on the wedding.

Before blaming, run the four questions: What am I Scared of? What am I Embarrassed about? What was I Expecting that I never said? What do I Need? Name the fear underneath instead of firing blame outward.
source: Morgan Burch — Dare to be SEEN

front: The truth is in the triggers
back: We resent people for doing things we don't feel allowed to do ourselves. And we expect others to react the way we would — but they're not us. When Megan's behavior stings, check whose rule got broken before assuming hers did.

front: Three lines that stop a fight
back: "That didn't feel good — what was your intention?" · "I'm feeling defensive — can you share that another way?" · "When you said that, I thought you meant ___ — what did you actually mean?" Each one swaps accusation for curiosity mid-conflict.

Trying to forgive keeps score; understanding closes the gap. A fast apology is often a way to skip the discomfort and “move on” — when I’m the hurt one, get curious about her intention before I demand one. Blame is drinking poison and expecting her to apologize for it. If I feel misunderstood, she probably does too — mirror first.

Connection at 10pm is built at 7am. A 6-second kiss, a 30-second hug, and specific gratitude ("thank you for packing lunches") maintain baseline connection all day. Gratitude is the #1 research predictor of marital satisfaction.

front: Sex is not a to-do item
back: 91% of parents say intimacy got harder after kids and the #1 blocker is time — so it slides down the list as a “luxury.” But it isn't another task to deprioritize like a bubble bath: it's quality time, vulnerability, and presence in one act, one of the most efficient forms of connection we have. If I can't prioritize it for us, prioritize it for the marriage the girls are learning from.

Morning coffee together before the day starts. Phone-free dinner. One thing I admire about her, out loud. A nightly "clean-up conversation" to clear small tensions before they compound. Small, daily, non-negotiable.

Emotional connection, touch, spiritual unity, sexual intimacy, finances, communication, friendship/flirting — each of us rates every area 1–10 alone, then compare. Pick ONE area for the year and set goals together. Don't fix everything; fix the lowest thing.

Disconnection doesn't arrive as a fight. It arrives as scrolling while she's mid-sentence, and a "how was your day" that stopped waiting for the answer. The smallest moments of attention — or inattention — compound harder than any argument.

It erodes trust through secrecy, desensitizes dopamine so real intimacy satisfies less, sets false expectations, and objectifies. Protecting my eyes is protecting our intimacy — this is maintenance, not paranoia.

front: The same argument means an unmet need
back: When a fight repeats, it's never about the topic — the dishes are a costume on a need (feeling valued, heard, chosen). Solve the need and the argument dies; win the topic and it comes back next week.
Being fully with my family is a choice, not a mood. The phone and the game are the test. Choose them on purpose.

A schedule and set of practices that create space to be with Jesus, become like Jesus, and do what Jesus did. The spiritual life doesn't happen in leftover time — design the rhythm like I design everything else.
source: Practicing the Way — Rule of Life

back: I don't need more information; I need inner formation. Habits flow from who I believe I am. Anything rooted in fear, guilt, or shame is a false identity — I was created on purpose, for a purpose, and made for more. Live from that.
PM: digest (no food an hour before bed), rest (airplane mode, disconnect), read. AM: water, movement, gratitude. Let go at night; step into thankfulness in the morning. Gratitude is the superpower.

Worship together, pray for each other's specific needs, keep God and family as the shared priority. Spiritual unity is a marriage area to actively score and grow — not a private track we each run alone.
Leaders can't reward what they can't see. Translate my team's work into the outcomes leaders actually care about — frame it in their language and tie the effort to impact, not activity.
When someone tries to redirect ownership of what I built, name it plainly and keep the receipts. Line up my backing before the conversation, not during it.

The Babble Hypothesis: people who talk most get read as leaders — and it derails careers. In the chair, my job is facilitating, not dominating. As the junior voice in a senior room: fewer, sharper contributions. Every meeting is a job interview.

Shielding an underperformer feels kind and demoralizes everyone else: the weakest player smells the fear, the strongest is updating their resume. Protecting one person's comfort at the team's expense is a leadership failure, not compassion.
Feel with them; don't take the problem from them. The line strong leaders never cross: caring about the person becoming carrying their accountability. Support the human, hold the standard.

Give people a level of care that's beyond reasonable — and treat adversity as the moment to create the story people retell. Problems handled extraordinarily build more loyalty than no problems at all.

front: The warrior mindset isn't the grind
back: It's not gritting teeth, hiding weakness, and working until collapse — that's the version being sold. It's disciplined stewardship of energy, honest self-assessment, and showing up ready. Recovery is part of the fight.

Document, delegate, and build systems that work when I am away. Also ask: who is learning to make the decisions I currently make? Give them practice explaining their judgment, not just following my instructions. Legacy includes people who can carry the work forward.
source: Eric Partaker; personal adaptation informed by Maxwell’s leadership principles

back: Start a remote 1:1 with genuine interest in the person. Follow their answer before moving to the agenda. Ask, listen, and remember what matters to them. Connection deserves attention even when I need nothing.
source: Cole Jennette — Small Talk Toolkit; personal adaptation informed by Maxwell’s leadership principles

back: Three questions at midyear: What did the first half teach me? What's working that I should double down on? What should I stop entirely? Look back on purpose before planning forward.

The hardest part of every payoff is convincing yourself to start. Introvert, anxious, doesn't matter — long-term ambitions die in comfortable avoidance, not in failure. Do the uncomfortable thing first.
Every reusable prompt: role, context, task, format, one example. Vague prompts get vague output. Always specify the format you want back.

Build: make it obvious, attractive, easy, satisfying. Break: make it invisible, unattractive, hard, unsatisfying. Every habit system I design — mine, my team's, my prompts' adoption — runs on these four dials.
source: James Clear — Atomic Habits cheat sheet

back: "I will [behavior] at [time] in [location]" beats vague intent. And chain new habits to existing ones: "After [current habit], I will [new habit]." The trigger does the remembering so willpower doesn't have to.

Scale any new habit down until it takes two minutes to start. Then design the environment so the right choice is the easy one — visible cues for good habits, friction for bad. The room beats the resolution.

Don't fix your whole life at once — it's almost impossible and it's how people fail. List the destructive habits, then pick ONE and be a sniper about it. Sequential wins compound; parallel fights collapse.

You can't white-knuckle a vice all day — give the urge a replacement job. Then trap yourself: tell two people you respect, put stakes on it ("if I fail, I pay you $X"). Make quitting more expensive than continuing.

Fighters get knocked out by the punch they didn't see. Name every habit that's stealing from the goals — write the list, feel the cost. Awareness isn't victory, but nobody wins a fight they don't know they're in.
Monthly audit: update all financial numbers, reflect on spending, review last month's goals, set next month's tied to the bigger plan. Systems without a review cadence quietly rot.
Each morning: today's top priorities, one thing to get excited about, a phrase to repeat under pressure, and who needs me on my A-game today. One page, five minutes, aims the whole day.
High intensity, low volume, 4–5x/week. Progressive overload beats novelty. The last hard rep is where the growth lives — don't leave it in the tank.
At least two full rest days per week, and never more than two or three training days in a row. Growth happens between sessions — the recovery structure IS the program, not an interruption to it.

front: How heavy: 2 honest reps in reserve
back: End working sets where you could TRULY do only 2 more reps. Could do 3+? Too light — add weight. Can't hit the bottom of the rep range? Too heavy. Then beat last cycle's weight when the split repeats.
Work up to the top of the rep range (e.g., 3×15) with clean form, then add a little weight and climb again. Slow and gradual on purpose — big jumps buy an early plateau and injury risk.

Some movements are great for almost everyone, some are a waste of time. Pick the best exercise per muscle: stable, easy to load progressively, full stretch under tension. Ruthlessly cut the mediocre ones.

Optional 5 minutes light cardio (especially after a desk day), then 5 minutes dynamic stretching for the half of the body being trained — arm circles, band pull-aparts, external rotations up top; leg swings below.

Cat cow (60s), world's greatest stretch (30s/side), Asian squat (30s hold + 30s rocking), half-kneeling thoracic rotations (30s), wall slides (60s). Five minutes daily unlocks lifts and undoes the desk.

front: Tendon pain: rest makes it worse
back: Tendons adapt to load; total rest deconditions them and the pain returns worse. Reduce the load and modify the movement — don't remove loading entirely. Manage it, don't hide from it.
Creatine monohydrate, protein powder, fish oil, a multivitamin. That's the science-backed list. Everything else is marketing until training, sleep, and diet are already dialed.

I don't have hours anymore — and I don't need them. The plan I'll actually repeat every week beats the optimal plan I'll skip. Consistency with a good program outruns perfection with an abandoned one.
Hit protein before anything else. It anchors satiety and protects muscle in a cut. Track it — don't estimate it.
Recomp near maintenance (~2,450) builds slowly. Cut cycles (~1,950–2,100) strip fat. Pick the phase on purpose. Don't drift between them.
Find maintenance, then +200 for a lean bulk or −500 for a cut. Protein: ~2g per kg (0.8g per lb) of bodyweight. Track daily — without tracking you're guessing, and guessing drifts.
Every chain has >14g-protein, <370-calorie options — Egg McMuffin is 300 cal / 17g protein. A rough day doesn't have to become a blown day. Know the plays before you're hungry in the drive-thru.

High-fiber, high-volume, lean-protein foods are the cut's best weapon: legumes, oats, berries, chia and flax, pears, brussels sprouts, sweet potatoes. Eat big, stay in deficit, skip the hunger spiral.

Before any trip decide: how am I getting there, how long, is there a kitchen? Pack protein snacks (jerky, bars, powder + shaker). Then on vacation — plan, relax, and enjoy the food. Stress costs more than a meal off plan.

Templates, not recipes: Greek yogurt + fruit, cottage cheese + fruit, blended protein ice cream (frozen fruit + whey + almond milk). Each lands 20g+ protein under ~300 calories. Keep the components stocked.

Plan the week, shop once, prep in one block, freeze extras for the air fryer. You make the healthy choice one time instead of twenty-one times. Decision fatigue — not knowledge — is what breaks diets.

Keep the house loaded with the staples: eggs, chicken, ground beef, salmon, Greek yogurt, rice, oats, sweet potato, spinach, berries, olive oil, nuts. When the kitchen is the environment design, the default meal is on-plan.

A boundary controls what I do (“I won’t keep talking when I’m yelled at”); a demand tries to control what she does. Boundaries invite the relationship to grow; demands try to force it into something more comfortable and suffocate it. State mine and hold myself to them — don’t issue orders for her.
source: Morgan Burch — Dare to be SEEN

front: Blame points to the fear underneath
back: The bigger my anger and the more aggressive my blame, the deeper the fear or embarrassment I’m protecting. “I just need YOU to change” is the tell. The SEEN method isn’t suppressing the feeling — it’s how I actually regulate it: name what I’m scared or embarrassed about instead of firing it outward.

Each of us carries an invisible account of how loved we feel right now — the sum of deposits and withdrawals. When it runs low we get reactive, defensive, easily sparked. Three jobs: make more small daily deposits, cut the withdrawals — the passive remarks (“guess I’ll wash your dish again”), micro-criticisms, and unrepaired arguments that drain it faster than big gestures fill it — and actually accept her deposits with warmth instead of missing them.

Weekly: repair anything unresolved, sync the schedule, and ask — what made you feel most connected this week? what felt hard? what can I do to support you? (listen without fixing, end positive). Quarterly: each rate satisfaction in the core areas so quiet dissatisfaction gets voiced. Yearly: revisit vision, goals, and values. Great teams huddle — schedule it, don’t wing it.

Most recurring issues never fully resolve — they’re rooted in personality and values, not solvable bugs. The real question isn’t “how do we fix this” but “can I live with this if it never changes?” Move perpetual problems from combat to dialogue; stop trying to win them.

Waking up, leaving the house, coming home, going to bed — these four moments set the emotional tone, and we’re most open to change at transitions. A positive goodbye and a real greeting at the door move the whole day. Small changes at the hinges produce big results.

How was today? How are you feeling right now? One thing you’re grateful for? One small thing that would feel good tomorrow? How can I be a better partner to you tomorrow? Five minutes, scheduled, door closed — and when she answers, listen and validate, don’t problem-solve.

front: Talk about the good stuff first
back: Most couples only talk about sex when something’s wrong, which makes the whole topic feel like a problem. Reverse it: open with a compliment about attraction, then a positively-rooted question (“what’s your favorite memory with me?”), then praise afterward. Build comfort on the good before ever raising a complaint.
source: Vanessa & Xander — How to Talk About Sex

back: Spontaneous drive: mental desire comes first, arousal follows. Responsive drive: arousal comes first, then the desire shows up — often only once things are already underway. Roughly 75% of men run spontaneous, ~30% of women responsive. Neither is broken; a responsive partner isn’t “not interested,” she just needs the on-ramp before the wanting arrives.

People initiate and want to be initiated in different ways: Excite Me (build a simmer, tease), Take Care of Me (choreplay, carry the load first), Play With Me (make me laugh, inside jokes), Desire Me (show me you want me), Connect With Me (emotional closeness first), Touch Me (physical first, not verbal). Learn Megan’s, lead with it — and know mine.

front: What she actually wants in bed
back: Not a performance. Four things: take your time and tease, focus on her pleasure, mix it up (most women don’t orgasm from intercourse alone — clitoral stimulation matters), and stay connected — eye contact, laughing, presence. Connection matters more than technique; the more connected she feels, the less the mechanics matter.

front: Whoever has lower desire initiates sometimes
back: Default scripts leave one person always initiating and the other always gatekeeping — which quietly builds resentment on both sides. Deliberately let the lower-desire partner initiate in a fun way sometimes. It resets the power balance and takes the pressure off the higher-desire partner to always ask.

front: Declutter the home to lower the noise
back: Simplified spaces are easier to manage, which means more rest and more focus on what matters — fewer environmental withdrawals on everyone’s nervous system. A calmer home is quietly a marriage and parenting intervention, not just tidiness.
source: 30 Days to a Home That Heals

front: Repair the rupture, not just the topic
back: Every couple fights; the ones who last are the ones who repair. After it cools, go back: name my part first without a “but,” name the impact (“that left you feeling dismissed”), and reconnect physically before re-litigating facts. The repair attempt matters more than who was right — it’s the strongest predictor of a marriage that survives.

Watch for the four patterns that predict divorce: criticism (attacking her character, not the behavior), contempt (eye-rolls, sarcasm, superiority — the single deadliest one), defensiveness (counter-attacking instead of hearing), and stonewalling (shutting down and going silent). Contempt is the one to hunt and kill on sight. The antidote to all four starts with me, not her.

front: Flooded means stop — same as the kids
back: When my heart’s pounding and I’m seeing red, my prefrontal cortex is offline — the exact amygdala hijack I know from the girls. I literally can’t hear her or think straight past ~100 bpm. Call it: “I need 20 minutes, I’m not leaving, I’m coming back.” Then actually self-soothe (don’t rehearse my case). Come back when regulated. Pushing through flooded only does damage.

“You never help” / “you always…” attacks her character and guarantees defensiveness. Instead: “When X happened, I felt Y, and I need Z.” Specific behavior, my feeling, a clear ask — no “always,” no “never,” no verdict on who she is. Same content, opposite outcome.

All day she makes tiny bids for connection — a comment about her day, a “look at this,” a sigh. Turning toward them (a real response, eye contact) instead of away (grunt, phone, “mhm”) is what quietly builds or drains the account. Masters of marriage catch the bids; the drift is just missed bids stacking up.

In conflict, stable couples run about five positive interactions for every negative one — and closer to 20-to-1 in ordinary life. One sharp remark needs several warm ones to offset it. I don’t have to be perfect in a fight; I have to keep the ratio positive. Repair, humor, affection, agreement all count.

Once resentment sets in, I read neutral acts as hostile — she forgot the milk “on purpose,” the short reply “means something.” That’s negative sentiment override, and it manufactures fights out of nothing. Default to the most generous plausible reading of what she did. Ask before I assume.

Desire isn’t just a gas pedal — it’s gas plus brakes. For most women the brakes matter more than the gas: stress, resentment, mental load, feeling unsafe, kids-might-wake, body image. “Not in the mood” usually means a brake is on, not that the gas is broken. The move is rarely more seduction — it’s finding and lifting the brake.
source: Nagoski, Come As You Are — sex-therapist addition

front: Her mental load is a brake — so service is foreplay
back: The invisible labor (planning, remembering, managing the kids) is one of the biggest desire-killers for mothers, and resentment about it is a brake that no amount of romance overrides. Megan’s love language is acts of service for a reason: carrying the load without being asked doesn’t just help — it removes the single biggest thing standing between her and wanting me.

When one of us wants more sex and one wants less, the natural moves make it worse: the pursuer pushes (which adds pressure = a brake), the distancer withdraws (which reads as rejection). The cycle, not either person, is the problem. Break it by taking pressure off and rebuilding no-strings connection — not by pursuing harder.

front: Love wants closeness; desire wants space
back: The paradox of long marriage: love thrives on safety, familiarity, and predictability — and desire needs mystery, novelty, and a little distance. Total domesticity can quietly extinguish eroticism even in a great partnership. Deliberately create separateness and newness: see her as her own person, not just co-parent and roommate.

If every touch is a down payment on sex, the lower-desire partner starts flinching from all touch to avoid the transaction. Give a lot of warmth that goes nowhere on purpose — hugs, hands, a kiss that isn’t a proposition. Safe, no-strings affection is what makes the pressure come off and desire have room to show up.

For responsive desire and busy-parent reality, waiting to both spontaneously feel it is a losing bet. Planning it isn’t clinical — it creates anticipation (a real accelerator) and guarantees the connection actually happens instead of getting crowded out. Put it on the calendar the way we protect anything that matters.

A contract is conditional and transactional — I’ll hold up my end if you hold up yours. A covenant is unconditional and permanent — I’m committed regardless. Marriage is covenant. When I catch myself keeping score or thinking “if she would just…,” that’s contract thinking creeping in. Lead with covenant even when I don’t feel it.

Ephesians 5: love her as Christ loved the church — by laying himself down for her. Headship is servanthood, not authority; it means dying to my own comfort and preference first. The question isn’t “is she meeting my needs” but “am I laying myself down for hers.” Marriage is a place I get discipled, not just a relationship I manage.

The word means to teach. When a consequence doesn’t work, it’s usually rooted in fear — and fear is a terrible long-term teacher. Punishment freezes the behavior in the moment (fight/flight), then it comes right back. I’m not trying to make them sorry; I’m trying to teach the next behavior.

No dessert tonight for throwing a ball at the park fails twice: a young brain can’t connect an event five hours later, and there’s no logical link between the ball and the cookie. The consequence has to connect to the behavior and land close to it. No connection, no correction.

A tantrum is behavioral — they still have access to the thinking brain, so hold the boundary calmly and flexibly (“not an option now, we can plan it for later”). A meltdown is the lower brain offline from overwhelm — no teaching gets through. Don’t try to fix it or reason; make it safe, say less, let it pass. Same map as my own flooding.

Most tantrums are transitions — the toddler brain hates surprise even for things that happen daily. PREP: Plan in advance, Reveal the plan, Explain the details (narrate what’s about to happen), and Put them in charge of one small thing (“blue jacket or purple?”). Warning the brain ahead of time prevents the threat response.

front: Give positive power with a choice
back: A lot of defiance is a bid for control. Instead of fighting it, hand over a small, bounded choice: “bed now — monkey or bear?” I make the big decision (that it’s bedtime); she makes the little one. Meets the need for power without surrendering the boundary.

In a sibling fight I don’t need the truth and I don’t rule. Get between them, pause, listen to each side, no pain too small, reflect it back (“you wanted the marker, he grabbed it”), empathy to both, then “any ideas how to fix it?” Being the judge robs them of the skill and makes one kid the winner. Stay neutral — throw water on the fire, not fuel.

With a strong-willed kid, the usual moves make it worse: hurrying and coercion (the frantic-morning spiral), and lecturing in the heat of anger. She isn’t broken and I’m not failing — strong will needs a different approach: fewer battles, more autonomy inside firm limits, and teaching only after everyone’s calm.

Decide the consequence before I speak. Then give one clear, concise instruction in a normal voice — no lecture, no hidden criticism. If she doesn’t respond, I act on the consequence instead of repeating myself. Repeating and re-appealing teaches her that my words are optional until I yell.

“I’ll do it myself!” and “you don’t care about me!” are bids for independence and leverage, not real accusations. Don’t argue or withdraw the request. Affirm and hold: “I care about you, and this still needs to happen.” Then feed the autonomy with a choice. Staying unshaken teaches the tactic doesn’t work.

Behavior is a symptom of what’s going on inside. When I correct, get to the root — was it fear, selfishness, feeling unseen? Then close the loop with real repair: name my part if I had one, forgive, restore. Our faith frame: obedience taught with love, not anger, and the relationship put back together every time.

front: Catch the good with a token economy
back: For a stretch where I’m only noticing misbehavior, a simple token system flips it: earn a token for the good I catch (respect, starting a chore unprompted, independent play), spend tokens on real rewards. It forces me to hunt for what’s going right instead of only reacting to what’s wrong.
source: Center of Psych — Reserve of Happiness

back: The master rule for feeding: I decide what, when, and where; she decides whether and how much. That’s the whole boundary. When I cross it — pushing bites, negotiating amounts — she pushes back and eats worse. Do my job, trust her to do hers. This is the foundation the rest of feeding sits on.

front: Food play: look → touch → smell → taste
back: A scared eater can’t jump to tasting. Move through stages: looking at the food, touching it, smelling/getting closer, then licking and tasting. Invite, never force — pressure re-triggers the fear. Any low-pressure interaction counts as exposure. For Emilia this is the on-ramp that meal-table pressure skips.

front: How I talk about food matters more than the plate
back: The goal isn’t broccoli tonight — it’s an adventurous eater for life. So I don’t pressure, bribe, or praise eating (“good job, two bites!” is still pressure), and I don’t become a short-order cook. Keep meal talk light and off the food. A positive table beats a cleaned plate every time.

Put the food in shared dishes and let her serve herself: “this is what we’re having, you can take as much as you want.” That’s the authoritative lane — high expectations plus high sensitivity, leadership with autonomy. Not authoritarian (clean your plate) and not permissive (what do you want instead?).

Grazing all day means never hungry enough for a real meal. Set 3 meals + 1–3 snacks at roughly the same times, water only in between. Predictable hunger and predictable structure cut the mealtime battles more than anything on the plate does.

front: Play is the work of childhood
back: Play is her language — it’s how she processes worries, learns, and feels connected to me. Commit to ~10 minutes of real play a day (all at once or in micro-moments). And when I need cooperation, reach for play first: make the shoe “talk,” sing it, turn it into a challenge. It’s hard for a kid to refuse an invitation to play.

front: Independent play is a skill I build
back: It’s not automatic — I build it. Declutter and rotate toys, set up a safe yes-space, then start small and stay close, and crucially don’t interrupt or direct when she’s absorbed. Every time I narrate or “improve” her play, I interrupt the muscle she’s growing. My job is presence, not participation.
source: Andrea Brambila — 10 Days to Independent Play

back: Rotate toys — keep 6–10 out, store the rest, swap every 1–4 weeks. Too many options overwhelm a kid the same way they overwhelm me, and an overwhelmed kid bounces instead of playing deep. Fewer, fresher toys = longer, richer independent play. Costs nothing but a bin.

Fast cuts, flashing color, and loud effects overload a developing nervous system — it’s like trying to focus in a room with strobe lights. Low-stim shows (slower pace, calm narration) leave her more regulated afterward. If there’s screen time, the content matters as much as the clock. AAP: about an hour a day at her age.

front: Connection play — and skip the tickling
back: Laughter releases oxytocin and resets a rough day. Physical games where I’m the one “losing” or bumbling (taco-roll, knee-bounce, shake-out-the-sillies) empower her while connecting us. Avoid tickling as the tool — it takes away her control even when she’s laughing. I want laughter plus power, not laughter plus helplessness.

Kid-centric outings (splash pad, sensory bins) often drain me and overstimulate them. What she actually wants is to do life with me — Home Depot, baking, picking up sticks, washing the car. Those fill both our cups instead of just taking from mine. Presence through ordinary tasks, not a produced event.

front: Kids must be taught to calm
back: Sending her to her room to “calm down” assumes a skill she doesn’t have yet. Calming is taught, not commanded. Practice breathing as play when she’s already calm — rainbow breaths, snake breaths, blowing bubbles — so the skill exists to reach for later. Design the capability in advance; don’t demand it mid-storm.

front: Co-regulation: I lend her my nervous system
back: A dysregulated kid borrows calm from a regulated adult. So the work is my body first — unclench, slow my breath, say less, model the calm without instructing her to breathe. Her system reads mine and shifts from fight-or-flight toward settle. I can’t talk her down; I can only bring her down with my own steadiness.

Every child has a different-size cup per sense. Low threshold = small cup, overwhelmed fast (loud rooms, tags, textures). Seeker = big cup with a hole, always craving input (crashing, spinning). Knowing each daughter’s profile tells me what triggers the dysregulation and what input actually calms her.

The kid who hangs, leans, climbs, and crashes into everything is self-medicating — proprioceptive input (pushing, pulling, carrying, squeezing) organizes and calms the nervous system. So give it on purpose: carry the groceries, push the laundry basket, animal walks, wall pushes, a crash pad. Movement before I need her regulated, not after.

Order the wind-down to actually work with her body: Connection (a little rough-and-tumble or a song) → Movement (rhythmic, predictable — blanket pulls, rocking) → Organizing/Calming (heavy work — bear hugs, kid-sandwich, tug-of-war) → Transition (lights low, books, snuggles, same closing line). Heavy work before bed, not screens.

front: Reading readiness is developmental, not age
back: Ready to read isn’t a birthday — it’s building blocks in order: pre-reading skills, letter sounds, phonemic awareness, blending, then reading. Push too early and I manufacture frustration; wait too long and I miss the interest. Watch for the signs (rhyming, pretend-reading, noticing letters), then start.

Four levers: Language (audiobooks, read to her, discuss it — build background knowledge), Engagement (books she actually cares about, so there’s a why), Affirmation (“you’re a reader who’s learning” — belief matters), and Decoding (systematic phonics, books she can actually read, sit beside her). Meaning and motivation, not just sounding out.

For a routine she resists, make it visual and let her finish it. Put a picture checklist right where she needs it (shoes by the door). Use chaining: I do all the steps but the last one and let her complete it, then hand her the last two, and so on backward until she owns the whole routine. Praise progress, not perfection.

front: Highly sensitive kids: be the safe space
back: Roughly 15–20% of kids are highly sensitive — Emilia’s anxiety profile fits. The rules flip: never punish the sensitivity, be the safe space instead of the threat, over-communicate and over-prepare her, invite don’t insist, and find the silver lining in the trait. Consequences work less well on these kids than safety and preparation do.
source: Jon Fogel — Highly Sensitive Kids Workshop

back: Instead of a flat no that trips the alarm, give a yes with a condition attached: “yes — as soon as shoes are on,” “yes, after dinner.” Same boundary, but her brain hears yes and the fight drains out of it. And when a question’s been asked and answered, I don’t re-argue it.

front: Hitting has a reason — and a three-part fix
back: At this age the theory-of-mind wiring isn’t built — she doesn’t fully grasp the other kid’s pain yet, so consequences alone won’t do it. The fix is three parts: gentle-hands redirect in the moment, calm conversations about it later, and actual practice — not just punishment. Teach the skill that’s missing.

front: Obedience is a bad ultimate goal
back: A kid who obeys any adult instantly and without question isn’t safe — they’re trainable by the wrong people. I don’t want blind compliance; I want cooperation plus a thinking kid who can eventually push back for good reasons. My discipline flow serves the relationship and the skill, not obedience for its own sake.

front: Kids do well if they can
back: The reframe under everything: misbehavior is usually a lagging skill or an unmet need, not defiance — it’s can’t, not won’t. When she’s melting down or stuck, ask “what skill is missing here?” instead of “how do I make her comply?” Solve for the gap and the behavior follows.

front: The repair matters more than the rupture
back: I will lose my cool sometimes. What the girls actually learn from is the repair afterward — me owning it, no “but you…,” naming the impact, reconnecting. A rupture followed by repair builds more security than never rupturing. It also models the accountability I want them to have. Same move I use with Megan.

Lower under control (2–3 seconds), then drive the concentric as fast as clean form allows. The lowering phase is where a lot of the growth stimulus lives — dropping the weight fast throws away free reps. Control down, explode up.

Volume, intensity, and frequency are the dials — and pushing one means easing another. I run high intensity and low volume, so my intensity is near-max and my per-session volume stays low on purpose. More of everything isn’t the goal; the right balance I can recover from is. Adding volume means I’d have to back off intensity or frequency.

front: Stay on a lift long enough to beat it
back: Swapping exercises every week feels productive but flattens the progression curve — the muscle never gets to adapt to the same movement twice. Pick the movement, then live on it for a block and chase the numbers up. Novelty is the enemy of overload.

Not every set to the bone. Isolation and machine work can go to true failure safely — that’s where the last-rep stimulus is cheap. Heavy compounds (squat, bench, deadlift) I leave 1–2 in reserve; failure there buys form breakdown and injury, not gains. Match proximity-to-failure to the risk of the lift.

Progressive overload isn’t a vibe — it’s a number I have to beat. Write down weight and reps every set, every session, and walk in aiming to top last time on something. If I’m not recording it, I’m not progressing it, I’m just working out.

Some movements give a lot of muscle stimulus for little systemic fatigue and joint cost; others wreck me for a mediocre return. Running low volume, I can’t afford junk fatigue — every exercise has to earn its spot on stimulus-to-fatigue, not ego. High reward, low wreckage.

Especially on isolation work, feeling the target muscle do the work beats moving the weight any way possible. Slow down, shorten the range if I have to, and actually contract the muscle I’m training. Moving weight isn’t the same as training the muscle.

front: Hit each muscle about twice a week
back: For growth, frequency of roughly 2x per muscle per week tends to beat blasting it once — more chances to accumulate quality volume and trigger protein synthesis. My split should have each muscle coming back around every 3–4 days, not once a week.

front: Train the core as an anti-mover too
back: Abs aren’t just crunches. The rectus flexes (crunches, leg raises), but the transverse and obliques resist movement — planks and Pallof presses train the anti-extension and anti-rotation that actually stabilize my spine under load. And abs progressive-overload like any muscle: add reps, then weight.

Recovery isn’t the absence of training — it’s where the adaptation happens, and sleep is the biggest lever in it. Under-sleeping blunts recovery, strength, and hunger control at the same time. Protecting sleep is protecting my gains, not competing with them. Same fight I already know matters.

front: Ramp into the first working set
back: Before the first heavy compound, pyramid up — something like 50% x for a few, 70% for a couple, 90% for one — to prime the pattern and the nervous system without adding fatigue. These feeder sets aren’t working sets; keep them easy. Warm the movement, don’t tax it.

A lean bulk means gaining about 0.5–0.75 lb per week — fast enough to add muscle, slow enough to keep fat off. Gaining much less means I’m leaving muscle on the table; much more means I’m just getting fat and will pay for it in the next cut. Aim for the slow climb, not the fast one.

Every calorie target is an estimate, including mine. The real program is the weekly trend: if the scale isn’t moving the direction the phase wants, nudge intake ~150 cal and reassess. Set the number, watch the trend, adjust. Don’t marry the starting number.

Once calories and protein are set, the carb-to-fat ratio is mostly preference — there’s no ratio that magically outperforms another. Stop optimizing the split and hit the two things that matter: total calories for the phase, and the protein floor. Simpler is more sustainable.

Build 80–90% of intake from whole foods for the fiber and micros; the remaining 10–20% can be whatever I want and it won’t hurt results if calories still fit. This is what makes it survivable long-term and what lets me eat with Megan and the girls without it being a production. Adherence beats purity.

Muscle protein synthesis responds better to several protein feedings than one big hit — aim for 3+ doses of ~25–40g through the day rather than backloading it all at dinner. Same daily total, better use of it. Anchor each meal with a protein.

Fat isn’t just calories — it’s raw material for testosterone and other hormones. Dropping it too low on an aggressive cut tanks hormones, mood, and recovery. Keep a fat floor even when slashing calories; pull more from carbs than from fat once fat is at a reasonable minimum.

Protecting T at my age isn’t a supplement — it’s the fundamentals stacked: 7–9 hours of sleep, managed stress (chronic cortisol suppresses it), heavy compound lifting, staying out of high body-fat ranges, and enough healthy fats, zinc, and vitamin D. The same habits I’m already chasing, pointed at hormones.

Walking is underrated cardio — a solid daily step count burns real calories without eating into lifting recovery the way hard cardio can. On a cut, my step count is a dial I can turn instead of cutting food further. Protect the daily walk; it’s doing more than it looks.

front: Hunger is manageable, not just endured
back: On a cut, beyond volume foods, the non-food levers matter: hydrate well, protect sleep (short sleep spikes hunger), use black coffee to blunt appetite, and keep protein high for satiety. Hunger is a signal to manage with tools, not a test of willpower to white-knuckle.

Alcohol is empty calories that also blunt recovery and testosterone and quietly loosen every food decision after the second drink. It’s not off-limits, but it isn’t free — decide before I’m out whether it fits the phase, the way I worked out for San Diego. Choose it, don’t default into it.

front: Adversity is a terrible thing to waste
back: I can’t control what hits the team or me — only how I respond and what I pull from it. Treat every setback as raw material for growth instead of something to just survive. The response is the part I own.

Guidara made his team memorize speeches for a new menu — and the whole experience went stale and got panned. Give people the what and the why, then let them execute in their own voice. Over-controlling the how kills the spark that made them worth hiring.

If every idea has to run through me, I’m the bottleneck and the team stops bringing their best. Let them run ideas that fit our values even when they aren’t how I’d do it. A good idea with full buy-in beats a great idea with minimal buy-in.

Drop the interrogation checklist. Look for three things: integrity, a real work ethic, and whether they’ll get along with the people already here. Then let new hires catch the culture behind the scenes before I put them on the front line.

Criticize the behavior, not the person. In private, never in public. Never emotional. Consistently. And always lead with a charitable assumption. One more: tell the team I’m raising the feedback bar before I start — raising it cold blindsides people.

The more I’ve poured into a project, a hire, or an approach, the harder it is to walk away — even when it’s clearly not working. What it cost to get here is gone either way. Decide on what’s true now, not on what I’ve already sunk into it.

McKinsey found people are up to 5x more effective in flow — yet most spend under 5% of work in it. Flow isn’t luck; it’s built from Time, Energy, Mentality, Proficiency, Organization (TEMPO). Protect a real block, kill interruptions, and let one hard thing absorb me fully.

A full calendar isn’t the same as a productive one. Time is fixed; energy is the variable I actually control — guard sleep, take real breaks, and put the hardest work where my energy peaks, not just where there’s a free slot. Match the task to the tank.

Missing once is an accident; missing twice is the start of a new habit — the wrong one. The rule isn’t perfection, it’s the fast return. Whatever slipped — the workout, the writing, the check-in — the only thing that matters is showing up for the very next rep.

Once a month, run the career pass: list my top 3–5 wins, save every piece of feedback I got, check last month’s goals against what I actually did, and set 2–3 new ones across role, development, and income. Nobody manages my growth for me — the cadence does.

When non-compliance or whining spikes my irritation, the reset is one line: she’s only five. She’s still a child, and acting like one is age-appropriate, not defiance aimed at me. Recalibrating the expectation to her actual developmental age drains most of the charge out of the trigger.

front: Father with the end in mind
back: Picture Emilia and Olivia at 25 — the women I hope they become — and parent today with that in view. Then the sobering math: I can actually count the weekends left before they leave home. Presence isn’t infinite. The evening I trade away to a screen is subtracted from a fixed total.

front: The rule is a trellis, not a cage
back: “Rule” of life sounds like legalism, but the root word meant trellis — the structure that lifts a vine so it bears the most fruit. My rhythms aren’t rules to pass or fail; they’re the support that frees me to abide. If a practice starts constricting instead of freeing, I revise it. Review the whole thing each season.
source: Practicing the Way — Rule of Life

back: The core disciplines a rule of life is built from: silence & solitude, Scripture, prayer, fasting, simplicity, Sabbath, and community. I don’t need all seven firing at once — pick the one or two this season actually needs and work them into the daily and weekly rhythm.
source: Practicing the Way — Rule of Life

front: Be the warrior my family needs
back: Five kinds of men: the Whiner stuck in his past, the Worrier afraid of the future, the Waiter hoping to be rescued, the Wounded suffering in silence — and the Warrior, who fights for his marriage and kids and cares more about legacy and character than his circumstances. Every morning I get to choose which one I’m going to be.
source: All Pro Dad — How to Be the Man

back: The pull is to measure myself by title, income, degrees — to prove I’m a man by out-achieving. But manhood isn’t how much I know or earn; it’s how much I grow in wisdom and how I show up for the people I’m responsible for. Character over credentials, every time.
source: All Pro Dad — How to Be the Man

front: Don’t shrink in the senior room
back: I can lead my own team with total confidence and still go quiet the moment I’m in the room with execs — letting the loudest voice win and swallowing the point I came in to make. That costs more than my confidence; worse decisions get made when I don’t take up my space. Ground myself before the high-stakes room and walk in already standing in it.

front: Workhorses get more work, not promoted
back: Being the most dependable person — the one who catches every dropped ball and works the weekend — can quietly trap me. I become indispensable to the team I’m in, so no one dares move me. Leaders who rise build the people and systems that run without them, and look up and out to become a trusted advisor to their boss. Promotion comes from proving my team succeeds when I’m not in the room.

front: Peer influence is earned, not charmed
back: Getting peers who don’t report to me to actually listen isn’t about charm, and my title means nothing to them. Influence across the org is earned — through credibility, following through, and being useful to them before I need anything. Bank the trust long before I need to spend it.

Real leadership calls rarely come in black and white — they’re a thousand shades of grey with no clean right answer. Waiting for certainty before I act is itself a decision, and usually a bad one. Make the best call I can with what I have, communicate the why, and adjust as it gets clearer.

I judge myself by relative position — how I stack up against the people right around me — not by any absolute standard. My scoreboard is relative, not absolute. That’s why growth feels like destruction: to grow I have to leave the small pond where I’m a big frog for a bigger one where I’m the dumbest in the room. That ego hit isn’t failure — it’s the cost of entry. Pay it with pride.

The core Stoic move: split everything into what’s up to me and what isn’t. My effort, my choices, my response — mine. Outcomes, other people, the past, what they think — not mine. Peace and power both come from pouring energy only into the first column and releasing my grip on the second.

Marcus Aurelius: the impediment to action advances action; what stands in the way becomes the way. The thing blocking me isn’t separate from the path — it IS the path. Every obstacle is raw material for the exact virtue the moment calls for: patience, courage, creativity. Don’t wish it away; work it.

front: Excellence is a habit, not an act
back: Arete — excellence — isn’t something I summon on the big day. It’s the accumulation of how I do the small, boring, unwatched things, over and over. I don’t rise to the occasion; I fall to the level of my habits. Build the habit and the moment takes care of itself.

front: Time is the one thing I can’t earn back
back: The wealthy buy cars, homes, jewels — but no one can buy back an hour. Time is the only truly non-renewable resource I have, and I spend it like it’s infinite. Guard it the way I’d guard the most valuable thing I own, because it is. Who and what I give it to is the realest budget I keep.

Seneca said we’re all slaves to something — food, phone, drink, ambition. But the chain isn’t fate. The same will that got captured can be turned. Change doesn’t start with a perfect plan; it starts with the decision, made now, that this is no longer who I am. Awareness plus a decision beats awareness alone.

front: Don’t defer the life I want
back: Memento mori isn’t morbid — it’s a forcing function. “Later” quietly assumes a supply of time I was never promised. The trip, the words to Megan, the thing I keep meaning to try — the honest question is why not now. Let death’s certainty make the living urgent instead of someday.

It’s easy to judge someone’s cowardice or failure and think I’d have done it right. But put in their exact position — their fear, their pressure, their formation — I’d likely have done the same. That humility does two things: it softens my contempt for others and it kills the excuse that I’m the exception. Judge my own actions first.

Before a real decision, write down the call, what I expect to happen, and why — then revisit it later. It separates decision quality from outcome luck (a good process can still get unlucky), kills hindsight bias, and over time shows me my actual patterns. Clearer thinking now, and something I can trust myself against later.

When I catch a lie and start interrogating — “did you lie to me?”, sharper voice, rapid-fire questions — the lesson isn’t honesty, it’s how to hide better next time. Kids mostly lie out of fear of my reaction. So I don’t ask a question I already know the answer to, and I don’t make telling the truth dangerous. Be safe enough that the truth feels possible.

front: Three sentences when a kid lies
back: Catch it: “I think something different happened. Can you help me understand?” — open a door, don’t accuse. When fear drove it: “I’m not going to get angry. I just need to know what actually happened.” — remove the threat before asking for truth. After the truth is out: “I can see you were worried about getting in trouble. That makes sense. And I still need honesty from you.” — the acknowledgment and the boundary in one breath.

front: Never break a promise to them
back: When Emilia reminds me I promised something — a sleepover, the park — and I’m tired and want to push it off, that’s the moment that matters. To me it’s a small reschedule; to her it’s whether my word means anything at all. Keep the promise, or don’t make it. Their trust in me is built one kept word at a time.

front: Break the cycle, don’t repeat it
back: The scary moment is watching my own worst reaction climb out of my kid — or catching myself doing the exact thing I swore I never would. I’m not doomed to repeat how I was parented, but awareness alone doesn’t break the pattern. It takes new skills rehearsed for the hard moments, and repair when I slip. The chain breaks in me.

The loud, melting-down kid gets all my attention. But the “good one,” the easy one, the mature one can be masking it — quietly learning to shrink her needs so she’s never a burden. I don’t mistake compliance for okay. Go looking for what a quiet Emilia or Olivia isn’t saying, and make sure being easy never becomes the price of my attention.

If my kids lack patience or self-control, the honest first place to look is me. They absorb my worst habits faster than any lesson I try to teach — how I handle traffic, my phone, my temper. I can’t lecture my way out of what I model. Self-regulation isn’t separate from parenting; it is parenting.

I opened up to Megan once, it came back in the next argument, so a part of me decided: never again, stay surface-level. That quietly costs the whole connection — she can’t know a man who won’t be known. Walking in already expecting it to be used against me is defeat before I speak. Make the pre-decision that if it stings, it won’t drop me. And when I share a struggle, bring the plan too, not just the problem.

front: Keep my voice in the hard conversation
back: When Megan — or anyone — makes a conversation difficult, I don’t have to pick between exploding and going silent. I can stay calm and still hold my position. Someone else being hard to talk to doesn’t mean I lose my voice or turn into someone I’m not. Say it with control, and say it anyway.

front: Be willing to be the bad guy
back: My job isn’t to be liked in the moment — it’s to raise them well. Some of the most loving answers are no, and a limit they need is worth their temporary anger. I don’t apologize for a boundary that’s good for them. Firm and kind aren’t opposites: hold the line, then reconnect.

After I finally say the hard thing, my body keeps replaying it and I feel worse, not lighter. That’s normal — doing the brave thing rarely feels like relief in the moment. The rattled, second-guessing feeling isn’t proof I got it wrong. Don’t undo a good decision just because it didn’t feel good.

A fixed mindset says ability is set, so every challenge is a test I can fail. A growth mindset says ability is built, so challenges are how I get better. Same event, opposite meaning. Catch myself treating a struggle as a verdict on who I am — and treat it as a rep instead.

front: Praise the effort, not the talent
back: Telling my girls (or myself) “you’re so smart” makes them protect the label by avoiding risk. Praising the strategy, the effort, the choice to keep going builds kids who take on hard things. Reward the process, not the person.

“I can’t do this” becomes “I can’t do this yet.” One word turns a dead end into a stage in a process. When Emilia hits a wall — or I do — “not yet” keeps the door open and points at the next attempt instead of the failure.

What predicts achievement over the long haul isn’t talent — it’s grit: holding the same top-level goal for years and not quitting when it’s boring or hard. Intensity is easy; the consistency of interest over time is what’s rare and decisive.

Talent × effort = skill. Skill × effort = achievement. Effort shows up in both equations — it builds the skill AND turns skill into results. The person grinding usually beats the gifted one who coasts. Bet on effort.

My all-or-nothing wiring loves starting things. Grit is the opposite muscle: going deeper on one thing for years instead of chasing the next shiny interest. Before starting something new, ask whether I’m building — or just fleeing boredom.

For anything past rote work, carrots and sticks backfire. Real motivation runs on three things: autonomy (control over how I work), mastery (getting visibly better), and purpose (it connects to something bigger). Build my work and my team around those, not bribes and threats.

Dangling a reward for creative work narrows focus and can kill the intrinsic interest that produced the good work. With my team: pay fairly, get money off the table, then drive with meaning and growth — not a bonus for every task.

You get closer to mastery but never fully arrive — and that’s the point. The joy is in the pursuit, not a finish line. Lifting, leading, faith: fall in love with the practice; the gap that never fully closes is what keeps it alive.

No dramatic moves — just small, smart choices, repeated, multiplied by time. Invisible for a while, then suddenly undeniable. The same math runs against me with small bad choices. Consistency on the little things is the whole game.

I own all of it — my choices, my reactions, my results. No blaming circumstances, my past, or anyone else. It’s a hard pill and a freeing one: if I’m the cause, I’m also the fix. Nothing changes until I take full ownership.

Whatever I want to improve — spending, calories, time, temper — track it honestly for a week first. The awareness alone shifts behavior, because I can’t fix what I refuse to look at. Measure the thing I’ve been avoiding.

The three hardest words to say. Faking certainty blocks the question that leads to a real answer. Admitting ignorance is where figuring it out begins — with my team, my kids, my faith. Trade fake confidence for honest curiosity.
source: Think Like a Freak — Levitt & Dubner

back: People don’t do what they say; they do what they’re rewarded for. When behavior confuses me — an employee, a kid, myself — stop moralizing and ask what incentive is actually driving it. Change the incentive and the behavior follows.
source: Think Like a Freak — Levitt & Dubner

back: Most people attack the problem as first stated. Re-ask the question — the real bottleneck usually isn’t where everyone’s looking. Before I solve, make sure I’m solving the right problem.
source: Think Like a Freak — Levitt & Dubner

back: Our culture worships the bold, fast, talkative “extrovert ideal,” but introverts bring deep focus, real listening, and thinking before speaking — and that’s a third to half of people. Not shyness to fix; a temperament to leverage.

Constant collaboration and open rooms can drown the deep thinking that real breakthroughs need. Guard alone-time for focused work — the quiet is where the good stuff gets made. Protect it like a meeting.

If I run introverted, people-heavy days drain a real battery, and I refill in solitude — not by pushing harder. Build in restorative niches: quiet mornings, a walk alone, a closed door. Manage the energy instead of white-knuckling it.
source: The Introvert Advantage — Marti Olsen Laney

back: Painful experiences are the raw material of growth — but only if I stop and reflect instead of just reacting. Don’t waste a mistake or a hard season; mine it for the principle it’s trying to teach. Reflect, extract, adjust.

My worst blind spots are the ones ego hides. Actively seek thoughtful people who disagree, weight their view by how credible they are on that topic, and stress-test my thinking against theirs. The goal is what’s true, not being right.

When I face a decision, I’ve usually faced its “type” before. Capture how I want to handle each type as a written principle, and decisions become repeatable instead of reinvented under pressure. Build my own playbook.

When people show me who they are or make their choices — let them. I burn enormous energy trying to control what others do and think. “Let them” releases the grip; “let me” points me back to the one thing I control: my own response.
source: The Let Them Theory — Mel Robbins

back: What other people think of me is mostly none of my business, and chasing approval hands them the wheel. Let them think what they’ll think; I steer by my values and the handful of people who actually matter.
source: The Let Them Theory — Mel Robbins

back: Every habit runs a loop: cue → routine → reward, with a craving powering it. Habits aren’t willpower failures; they’re grooves. To change one, first see the loop I’m actually running — including the reward the bad habit is quietly paying me.
source: The Power of Habit — Charles Duhigg

front: Keep the cue and reward, swap the routine
back: I can’t erase a habit, but I can redirect it: keep the same cue and same reward, change the routine in between. Bored at night (cue) wanting to unwind (reward) → swap “open a game” for a routine that still pays off.
source: The Power of Habit — Charles Duhigg

back: Some habits quietly pull others into line — exercise, a made bed, a family dinner. Change one keystone habit and a cascade follows. Instead of fixing everything at once, find the one habit that drags the rest upward.
source: The Power of Habit — Charles Duhigg

back: “Should I do this — yes or no?” is a trap; a whether-or-not decision means I’ve only found one option. Force a couple more (What else could I do? What would I tell a friend?). Widen the options before I pick.

I gather info that confirms what I already want. Instead, hunt for disconfirming evidence, run a small experiment, or ask someone who’ll tell me I’m wrong. A quick pre-mortem — “it’s a year later and this failed, why?” — surfaces the truth cheaply.

Short-term emotion hijacks decisions. Ask: how will I feel about this in 10 minutes, 10 months, and 10 years? The gut-panic usually shrinks at the longer ranges, and the right call gets clearer once I zoom out.

The core distinction: an asset puts money in my pocket, a liability takes it out. The rich buy income-producing assets; the middle class buys liabilities they think are assets (the bigger house, the nicer car). Every dollar is a little worker — spend it hiring more workers.
source: Rich Dad Poor Dad — Robert Kiyosaki

back: Working for money is the treadmill; the goal is to own assets that earn whether or not I show up. Financial freedom is when passive income covers my expenses. Build the machine that pays me, so my time stops being the only thing for sale.
source: Rich Dad Poor Dad — Robert Kiyosaki

front: Financial literacy is the real education
back: It’s not how much I make, it’s how much I keep and how hard it works. Cash flow, assets, taxes, how money actually moves — that knowledge matters more than income. Fear and “playing it safe” keep smart people broke; learn the game and take intelligent risk.
source: Rich Dad Poor Dad — Robert Kiyosaki

back: Willpower fails; systems don’t. Set automatic transfers on payday — to investments, savings, bills — so the right thing happens without a decision. Design the system once and let it run. What’s automated gets done.
source: I Will Teach You to Be Rich — Ramit Sethi

back: Spend extravagantly on the few things I truly love, and cut costs mercilessly on everything I don’t. Guilt-free spending isn’t the enemy — unexamined spending is. Decide what my money is FOR, then fund that on purpose.
source: I Will Teach You to Be Rich — Ramit Sethi

back: Agonizing over $3 lattes while ignoring the 5–10 big levers — savings rate, housing, salary, fees — is backwards. Get the handful of big decisions right and the small stuff barely matters. And a “rich life” is personal: define mine instead of copying anyone else’s.
source: I Will Teach You to Be Rich — Ramit Sethi

back: My leadership can become a bottleneck. Where am I limiting clarity, trust, decisions, or ownership? Improve that constraint while also checking staffing, tools, and incentives.
source: The 21 Irrefutable Laws — John Maxwell; personal adaptation informed by Maxwell’s leadership principles

back: Not title, not position, not the org chart — leadership is influence, nothing more, nothing less. If no one’s following, I’m just taking a walk. Influence is earned through trust and track record, not granted by a badge.

Leaders are made in small daily disciplines, not in a single event or promotion. What I do consistently — reading, reflecting, reps — compounds into capacity. Lead myself well every day and the growth accrues.

front: Your inner circle sets your ceiling
back: Build relationships with people whose strengths complement mine and who can challenge me honestly. Listen to different perspectives, welcome disagreement, and contribute to their growth too. Strong leadership is shared, not carried alone.
source: The 21 Irrefutable Laws — John Maxwell; personal adaptation informed by Maxwell’s leadership principles

back: The most important thing I bring to a tense room isn’t answers — it’s my own calm. When everyone’s reactive, the leader who stays steady and self-regulated lowers the whole system’s anxiety. Manage my reactivity first; it’s contagious either way.
source: A Failure of Nerve — Edwin Friedman

back: Lead from my own clear values instead of bending to whoever’s most upset. Staying connected to people WITHOUT absorbing their emotions or caving to pressure is the whole skill. Be my own person while staying in relationship.
source: A Failure of Nerve — Edwin Friedman

front: Don’t let the most anxious set the pace
back: Systems organize around their most reactive, dependent, or demanding member. If I keep adapting to them, I hand them control. Lead toward strength and health, not toward whoever complains loudest.
source: A Failure of Nerve — Edwin Friedman

back: When I make a genuine change or hold a hard line, pushback isn’t proof I’m wrong — it’s the system trying to pull me back to normal. Staying steady THROUGH the resistance is what makes the change stick. Don’t cave at the sabotage.
source: A Failure of Nerve — Edwin Friedman

front: Be proactive: work your circle of influence
back: Between what happens and how I respond is a gap — and my freedom lives there. Proactive people pour energy into what they can affect; reactive people burn out on what they can’t. Spend myself on the part I control.

front: Begin with the end in mind
back: Start every effort with a clear picture of the destination. Write the ending first — the man, father, and leader I want to have been — and let it steer today’s choices. Make sure the ladder’s against the right wall before I climb fast.

Important-but-not-urgent work — health, relationships, planning, growth — gets crowded out by urgent noise. Schedule that Quadrant II work first, on purpose, or it never happens. Don’t prioritize my schedule; schedule my priorities.

Most people listen to reply, not to understand. Truly grasp the other person’s view before I push mine — with Megan, the girls, my team. Understanding first lowers defenses and earns me the right to be heard.

front: Find your voice, help others find theirs
back: Beyond effectiveness is greatness: find my voice — where my talent, passion, need, and conscience meet — then inspire the people I lead to find theirs. Leadership is communicating others’ worth so clearly they come to see it in themselves.

Criticism puts people on the defensive and rarely changes them — it just breeds resentment. Any fool can condemn; it takes character to understand and encourage instead. Lead with appreciation, not fault-finding.
source: How to Win Friends & Influence People — Dale Carnegie

back: The deepest human craving is to feel important. Sincere, specific appreciation — not flattery — is the cheapest powerful thing I can give. Catch people doing things right and say so, at work and at home.
source: How to Win Friends & Influence People — Dale Carnegie

back: To move anyone, first arouse in them an eager want — talk in terms of what THEY care about, not what I want. Seeing it from the other person’s point of view is the closest thing to a magic formula. Frame my ask in their interests.
source: How to Win Friends & Influence People — Dale Carnegie

back: I make more friends in two months by being interested in people than in two years trying to make them interested in me. Ask, listen, remember the details. Real curiosity about others is magnetic — and rare.
source: How to Win Friends & Influence People — Dale Carnegie

back: Incremental goals produce incremental effort. A target an order of magnitude bigger forces a different question — not “how do I work harder” but “what would have to be true?” — and usually a smarter, systemized answer. Let the bigger vision recruit the better strategy.

front: Get it out of your head
back: My mind is for having ideas, not holding them. Capture every open loop — task, idea, commitment — into one trusted system outside my head, so my brain stops nagging and starts thinking. Open loops drain focus until they’re written down.
“Plan the trip” stalls; “text Megan possible dates” moves. Every open loop needs a concrete physical next action — the smallest real step. Vague projects don’t get done; next actions do.

If a task takes less than two minutes, do it now rather than tracking it — filing it costs more than doing it. Everything bigger gets deferred into the system or delegated. Small stuff, handled on contact.

Being busy is a form of laziness — lazy thinking and indiscriminate action. Doing something well doesn’t make it worth doing. Before I optimize a task, ask whether it should exist at all. Cut first, then streamline what’s left.

Work expands to fill the time available. Give a task all day and it takes all day; give it two hours and it’s done in two. Set short, almost-uncomfortable deadlines to force focus and cut the fluff. Constrain the time on purpose.

Most of what I consume — news, feeds, noise — is neither important nor actionable, just anxiety with a refresh button. Ruthlessly cut inputs that don’t serve a decision I’m actually making. Protect attention like the scarce resource it is.

front: There’s no recipe for the hard things
back: The easy things have formulas. The genuinely hard things — laying someone off, holding on when it looks hopeless, the call with no good option — have none. The struggle IS the job. Stop waiting for a clean answer that isn’t coming and lead through the mess.
source: The Hard Thing About Hard Things — Ben Horowitz

front: People, products, profits — in that order
back: Take care of the people first; if the people are right, they build the product and the product drives the profit. Reverse the order and it all erodes. How I treat my team isn’t soft — it’s the foundation everything else stands on.
source: The Hard Thing About Hard Things — Ben Horowitz

back: Trust is built by sharing the bad news, not hiding it. People can handle hard truth; what they can’t handle is being spun or managed. Say the real thing plainly — morale survives honesty far better than it survives a cover-up.
source: The Hard Thing About Hard Things — Ben Horowitz

back: When a big feeling has flooded Emilia, help her put it into words and tell the story of what happened. Naming the emotion brings the logical brain online to calm the emotional one. I can’t reason a flooded kid down, but I can help her name her way back.

The “upstairs” thinking brain — self-control, planning, empathy — is under construction until the mid-20s. When my kid melts down, her downstairs reactive brain has taken over. She’s not giving me a hard time; her upstairs brain literally isn’t built yet.

In a hot moment I can trigger the reactive downstairs brain with commands and threats, or engage the thinking upstairs brain with a question or a choice. “What’s your plan for this?” beats barking an order — it recruits the part of her I actually want running.

front: Acknowledge the wish, hold the limit
back: “No” lands better once the feeling is heard. “You wish you could have ice cream right now — you love it. It’s almost dinner, so it’s a treat tomorrow.” Giving her the wish in words, even in fantasy, softens the limit without moving it.
source: How to Talk So Little Kids Will Listen — Faber & King

back: Little kids live in play, so a command breeds a battle but a game gets buy-in. Make the toothbrush talk, race to the car, let the shirt “gobble” her arm. Silliness isn’t being a pushover — it’s the shortest path through resistance.
source: How to Talk So Little Kids Will Listen — Faber & King

back: Instead of “Why do you always leave your shoes there?” just describe it: “I see shoes in the doorway.” Stating the problem without the accusation invites her to fix it instead of defend herself. Describe what I see; let her solve it.
source: How to Talk So Little Kids Will Listen — Faber & King

back: Every time I let Emilia avoid the scary thing or pile on reassurance, the worry gets a little stronger — accommodation feeds it. Love isn’t removing the fear; it’s walking her toward it. Comfort the child, don’t obey the anxiety.
source: Freeing Your Child from Anxiety — Tamar Chansky

back: Give the worry a name and make it a separate thing — a worry bully, a brain glitch — so it’s Emilia-and-me against the worry, not me against Emilia. “That’s your worry brain talking, not the truth.” Then she can talk back to it instead of believing it.
source: Freeing Your Child from Anxiety — Tamar Chansky

back: Facing a fear all at once overwhelms; facing it in small steps builds proof. Break the scary thing into a ladder and take one rung at a time, each success becoming evidence she can handle the next. Brave is built gradually, not demanded.
source: Freeing Your Child from Anxiety — Tamar Chansky

front: Validate the feeling, back her ability
back: Two things at once: “I know this feels really scary” (I take the feeling seriously) AND “and I know you can handle it” (I believe in her). Not dismissing with “you’re fine,” not rescuing — empathy plus confidence is what grows courage.
source: Freeing Your Child from Anxiety — Tamar Chansky

front: Talk about sex outside the bedroom
back: The worst time to work on our sex life is in the moment, half-clothed and vulnerable. Have low-pressure conversations in normal daylight — what we each like, want, miss. What we can talk about calmly, we can actually change.

Bring the posture of teammates exploring, not a critic grading. “I’d love to try…” and “what feels good to you?” open doors that complaints slam shut. We’re on the same side of this, figuring it out together.

God, man, Christ, response: God is our holy Creator and King; we’ve all sinned and stand guilty; Jesus lived, died, and rose to take that judgment and give us his righteousness; and the call is to repent and trust him. That’s the frame the whole message hangs on.
source: What Is the Gospel? — Greg Gilbert

front: The gospel is news, not advice
back: Most religion is advice — things to do. The gospel is news — something already done. Not “try harder and be good enough,” but “Christ has done it, now believe.” I don’t work to earn it; I rest in what’s finished and let that reshape me.
source: What Is the Gospel? — Greg Gilbert

back: I can run the Christian life on my own effort and quietly forget the Holy Spirit is meant to be the power source. A life that actually depends on the Spirit looks different — less white-knuckling, more surrender. Stop striving alone; ask and yield.

If my life only makes sense because God is real, I’m leaning on the Spirit. If it runs fine on my own competence and comfort, maybe I’m not. Following him will sometimes look risky and inconvenient — that’s the point, not a malfunction.

The heart cannot love what the mind does not know. Feelings-first Bible study fizzles; do the work of understanding the text — what it says, what it means — and let real knowledge of God fuel real love for him. Comprehension before application.

front: The Bible is about God, not me
back: I come to Scripture asking “what does this say about me?” when the first question is “what does this reveal about God?” See his character first; my identity and marching orders only come into focus after I’ve seen him clearly.

Exodus: God doesn’t just free his people FROM slavery, he frees them FOR himself — to dwell among them. Salvation isn’t mainly about my comfort or escape; it’s about being brought near to God. He rescues, then he comes to dwell.

front: God wins — live with the end in view
back: Revelation pulls back the curtain: however dark it looks now, God is on the throne and he wins. That certain ending is meant to steady me in today’s trial — worship over worry, faithfulness over fear. Live backward from the victory that’s already sure.
