Don’t just graze the comfortable, familiar passages — read through all of Scripture systematically. The parts I’d skip are usually the ones that stretch me most, and the whole story only makes sense whole. A little every day, cover to cover.

front: Talk to myself like a friend
back: When I mess up, my instinct is to lay into myself — but harsh self-criticism triggers shame and shutdown, not change. Talking to myself the way I would a friend I’m rooting for actually produces more follow-through. Kindness isn’t going soft; it’s what keeps me in the game.

My all-or-nothing wiring hears one missed workout or one bad day as “I’ve blown it, may as well quit.” But one data point isn’t the trend — the spiral does far more damage than the slip. Get back on the horse without the self-punishment tax. Missing once is human; quitting is the only real failure.

front: Rest is part of the work
back: Recovery isn’t the reward I earn after the work — it’s where the growth actually happens, in muscle and mind alike. My worth isn’t my output. Building in real rest breaks the burnout-then-crash cycle all-or-nothing people fall into. Schedule the rest before I need rescuing by it.

My standing with God doesn’t rise on a good day or fall on a bad one — grace already settled it. I’m not auditioning for love I have to earn; I’m living from love I already have. For a striver like me, this is the ground to stand on when I inevitably fall short.

God built rest into the week and commanded it — one day to stop producing. Sabbath is a weekly declaration that the world holds together without me and that I’m not what I make. Stopping when there’s still more to do is an act of trust, not laziness. Protect a real day off.

front: Train the heart, not just the muscles
back: My plan is 100% resistance — great for muscle, close to useless for cardiovascular fitness. VO₂max (aerobic capacity) is one of the strongest predictors of how long and how well I live. All the lifting in the world won’t cover this gap. Add dedicated cardio like it matters, because it does.

Most of my cardio should be easy — conversational pace, ~60–70% max heart rate, 2–3 sessions a week — to build the aerobic engine and recovery. My daily walks count if I push the pace. Then add one harder session a week of intervals to drive VO₂max up. Easy base, occasional peak.

Every 4–8 weeks, take a lighter week — cut volume, back off intensity — so accumulated fatigue clears and I come back stronger. Planned recovery prevents the forced kind: injury, stalls, burnout. For a hard-charger, the deload is the discipline, not the weakness.

front: Faith is caught more than taught
back: Emilia and Olivia will absorb my actual walk with God — do they see me pray, admit when I’m wrong, worship, lean on him under stress? — far more than any lesson I assign. I can’t hand down a faith I’m only performing. Let them watch the real thing.

front: Talk about God in the ordinary
back: Faith passes in the everyday moments — in the car, at meals, at bedtime — not just in formal sit-downs. Weave him into normal life so knowing God feels woven in, not bolted on. A natural comment beats a lecture every time.

front: Give them room to own it
back: My job isn’t to manufacture my daughters’ faith — I can’t — it’s to point them to Christ and let it become theirs, not just inherited rule-following. Welcome their hard questions instead of fearing them. Real faith is owned, not forced.

Praying with Megan — even short, even awkward — reaches a deeper intimacy than any date night. Sharing what we’re each carrying before God binds us in a way logistics never will. Lead it gently and don’t wait to feel like it; start small and keep it up.

Even as the CFP of the house, the point isn’t my competence — it’s that Megan and I face money as teammates. Regular, calm talks about goals, spending, and fears prevent the silent resentment finances breed. Same team, same page, on purpose.

Beyond schedules and to-dos, we need a shared future to point at — what we want for the family in one year, five, ten. Couples drift when the dreaming stops and it’s all logistics. Keep a living picture of the life we’re building together.

Knowing Megan’s inner world — her current stresses, hopes, what’s on her mind this week — isn’t a one-time achievement. She changes; keep asking and stay curious so I’m loving the woman she is now, not the one from five years ago. Update the map.

Naming what I’m thankful for — a few specific things, regularly — measurably lifts mood and starves the comparison and “never enough” machine. It’s not fluff; it’s one of the most evidence-backed habits there is. End the day with three things that went right.

The longest study of human happiness found the number-one predictor of a good life isn’t money, status, or achievement — it’s the quality of close relationships. All my optimizing means little if I neglect Megan, the girls, and real friends. Invest there first.

front: Prayer: talk to him like he’s there
back: Prayer isn’t a crisis hotline or a performance — it’s an ongoing, honest conversation. Ask, thank, confess, and actually listen. Keep it constant and real rather than eloquent. The point isn’t good words; it’s a real relationship kept open.

Christianity was never meant to be solo. I need a real community that knows me, spurs me on, and catches me when I drift — not just sermons I consume from a distance. Belong to a church body; be known, not anonymous.

The ability to focus without distraction on one demanding thing is rare, valuable, and getting rarer. Batch the shallow stuff — email, pings — kill notifications, and protect long uninterrupted blocks for the work that actually matters. Attention is the asset; guard it.

Hand off real ownership with an agreed learning goal, decision authority, clear boundaries, and a check-in. Ask what capability this person wants to build, then choose a stretch responsibility together. Support their judgment without taking the work back.
source: Multipliers — Liz Wiseman; personal adaptation informed by Maxwell’s leadership principles

back: My protein is dialed, but fiber and plants are the quiet gap — they drive gut health, fullness, and long-term disease protection. Aim for a big volume of vegetables and plenty of fiber daily, with variety across the week. Feed the gut, not just the muscle.

Most of us treat intercourse as the main event, but for most women it isn’t the most pleasurable part — and few reach orgasm from penetration alone. Treat foreplay as equal to intercourse, not a rushed preamble, and keep some clitoral stimulation going during intercourse itself, not only before. Build the whole thing around her pleasure, not just the finish.

front: Orgasm is a team goal, not a given
back: The unspoken script ends things at my finish. Flip it: her orgasm and mine are a shared project we both look out for, and neither is guaranteed or owed. And never make a specific outcome a target to hit — pressure backfires. Aim at connection and pleasure and let the rest follow.

front: Her quiet can be a good sign
back: If Megan goes quiet I read it as “it’s not working” — but many women go inward to focus on sensation, and silence often means the opposite. Instead of guessing, agree on a simple cue ahead of time: a hand squeeze that means “yes, this.” Then I’m not performing in the dark.

If I lose my erection mid-moment, that’s an arousal-level thing, not a verdict on me or on us — no emergency. The line that dissolves the pressure for both of us: “Is this feeling good for you? I’m happy to keep going as long as you are.” Curiosity about her beats panic about me.

front: Get out of my head, into the moment
back: Spectatoring — scoring my own performance and her reactions from the outside — kills the very thing I’m anxious about. The fix is to drop back into sensation and my own pleasure. I’m allowed to enjoy this for its own sake, not monitor it. Feel it, don’t grade it.
source: Vanessa & Xander Marin — Supercharge Your Confidence

front: Schedule it earlier, build the anticipation
back: Scheduling sex isn’t unromantic — it protects the time and lets us build anticipation by flirting all day. One tweak: put it earlier in the evening, not right before sleep when we’re both fried and set up to disappoint each other. Plan it for when we’ve still got something in the tank.
source: Vanessa & Xander Marin — Bring Your Sex Life Back To Life

back: “What do you like?” is hard to answer in the moment. Easier: offer a comparison — “this, or this?” — and let her pick, back and forth, dialing it in like Goldilocks. And to redirect without criticizing: “can you do that again, but a little slower?” Works just as well when she says it to me.

front: Frame grooming as desire, not criticism
back: “You need to shower” stings; “I want you — go get cleaned up for me first” lands. Same ask, framed as wanting rather than faulting. Shower together as foreplay, or gift a scent I love. And it runs both ways — my scratchy beard is her comfort too, so the beard oil isn’t just cosmetic.

Hanging back and waiting for Megan to lead can feel considerate, but it dumps all the vulnerability on one of us — and usually leaves neither of us feeling desired. Sharing the risk of reaching for her IS the respect. If we’re both stuck in a standstill, someone just has to go first — even flip a coin.
source: Vanessa & Xander Marin — The Art of Initiation

back: Some people need to feel emotionally close before they want sex; others feel close through sex. Megan and I may run opposite ways, and neither is wrong. Naming which each of us is ends a lot of silent frustration — I can give her the connection she needs first, and she can see that sex is partly how I connect.
source: Vanessa & Xander Marin — Your Best Week Ever

front: Timeout WITH her, not away from her
back: Sending a kid off alone to “think about it” registers in her brain close to physical pain, and it buys compliance through a small dose of love-withdrawal — not real understanding. Instead, pause WITH Emilia: stay present, ride it out beside her, lead with “I’ve got you” before any problem-solving. Connection before correction.

Not a punishment spot — a cozy reset space with a few comforting things she can go to when emotions get big. It gives her somewhere to regulate that isn’t isolation or exile. A place to come back to center, chosen, not a bench she’s sentenced to.

If my warmth and attention only show up when she’s behaving or achieving, I’m quietly teaching her that love has conditions. Praise the good, sure — but she should never have to earn my affection. She ought to feel most secure in me exactly when she’s at her worst.

Even when I doubt the facts around it, her emotional report deserves belief — “that sounds really hard” beats “you’re overreacting.” And being available matters more than extracting a talk on my schedule: leave the door open, don’t pry it. She’ll come when she trusts I’ll believe her.

My instinct is to swoop in the second she’s frustrated, but the struggle itself is where capability gets built. Tolerating a little frustration — the puzzle, the zipper, the hard feeling — grows her more than my rescue does. Stay close and encouraging, but don’t rob her of the win by doing it for her.

When Emilia does something maddening, the move is to investigate it — what’s underneath this? — instead of reacting to the surface. Same lens on my own flash of anger: get curious about what just got triggered in me. Curiosity turns a power struggle into a puzzle I can actually solve.

A meltdown is immaturity, not an attack on me — but my body doesn’t know that until I tell it. Before I respond, physically shake off the stress (or ground with 5-4-3-2-1) and name my own emotion out loud: “I’m feeling really frustrated right now.” I can’t calm her nervous system with a hijacked one of my own.

front: No bad feelings — only limits on behavior
back: Every emotion she has is allowed, even the ugly ones; it’s the behavior that has limits. “You’re allowed to be furious. You’re not allowed to hit.” I don’t need to argue her out of the feeling — I validate the feeling AND hold the line on the action. Both, at once.

Telling a flooded kid to “just calm down and breathe” almost never works — it’s too abstract mid-meltdown. Give her something concrete and playful instead: blow out each “candle” finger one at a time, or smell-the-flower then blow-the-pinwheel. Same deep breath, but a version her brain can actually follow.
